title: TDD-rant
author: affabledrunk
selftext:
I share this because I suspect many people here are not actual SWEs.

TDD = test driver development

Its what all modern SW orgs do. Lots of automated unit and integration tests.

I'd done personal projects, tools, games whatever but I never ever bothered writing tests.

What's great about these genai tools is that they want write tests for you. Let them, it's amazing for code quality and robsutness and so little cost.

In my games, I mostly use straight node and i'm loving all these playwright tests which codex generates, really helpful. 

I have a question for those people using engine like UE or Godot, do they provide UI testing frameworks? If they do, you should exploit them. Its amazing.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
TDD means test-driven development. It’s where you write the tests first.

Very few software orgs work this way.

replies.author: affabledrunk
replies.body: I didn't mean that level of test cult,  perhaps I should have used a different terminology. People often use TDD to decribe standard unit test culture thats the baseline for most SW orgs I've seen (like Google et al). I just meant, you should never ship a feature without unit tests.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: People don’t use TDD that way. It just means tests first, code afterwards. That’s what TDD means. TDD = tests first, code second.

replies.author: ThinkingOutLoud-7742
replies.body: Everybody unit tests, but not every project benefits from TDD. Tests are good to verify that nothing breaks when implementing future changes. Sometimes it makes sense to do TDD. If you have a feature with well defined specs, and you know that this isn’t going to change in the future, then TDD works by turning the specs into tests and guiding the development process. If you don’t know \*precisely\* what the specs are, as is often the case when building a gameplay loop, then the development process will likely include a lot of iteration. TDD then wastes a lot of time by writing tests for features that will later be changed.

replies.author: just_a_timetraveller
replies.body: That's not TDD. TDD is a very specific style of programming from the extreme programming days.

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
Yeah, we tried it at the place I worked at, and really only one dev there was able to do it right. And it wasn't me. 

It just takes more planning than I'm used to. You write the test case first, see it fail, then start building the code until that test passes.

I get the approach to a degree - everything gets created as testable parts of the code. Lots of tests become hard to write after the fact because so many functions can't be tested in isolation.

But it presents different problems - trying to tie all these testable but unrelated functions into an actual code flow. And then having a test for that too. You end up with code that is easily testable for individual functions but not for the code flow as a whole. 

At least, that's how it always ended up for me. I like to get something going and see what shape the code is going to take. When I have a working version, the important parts get tests, possibly with a flag to prevent actually making costly Api calls or something. It's less coverage, but much faster for me.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: I think it makes sense in some specific scenarios, like writing parsers. When you’re writing a parser, maybe the test cases are super easy to write out, and test a big chunk of code in the process. But yeah, TDD has a lot of problems and is hard to put into practice.

replies.author: just_a_timetraveller
replies.body: Exactly this. I think if you want to do TDD with Ai development maybe you write the tests by hand first, and then ask the AI to create the functionality within the parameters of the test. That way you can really force the interfaces you want and also understand more of what the AI is trying to do.

comments.author: InsolentCoolRadio
comments.body:
Robert C. Martin had an interesting post recently where he advocated for something I think he called ‘mutation testing’ where essentially you clone your repo and deploy “mutants” into the code to break it and see if the AI agent generates tests actually flag that the code is broken and test what they claim they’re testing.

It’s on my list of things to experiment with.

Recently I’ve been having my agent deploy a sub-agent to write and a second sub-agent to proofread and make sure the first agent is doing what it’s supposed to, although I’ve mostly used that for updating game design documents I imagine it should work for code as well.

comments.author: AgenticGameDev
comments.body:
I use playmode tests and especially E2E test to drive the development. It’s great. I describe what needs to be tested and the ai develop the code and then the test. This works great once the architecture is in place and you want to start with gluing things together. The base modules inmostly design the other way. Describe the architecture and then let the agent implement it and then write the test for it.

I would say classical TDD is not how ai think so it’s very slow even if it can do it it’s not native to the stepwise forward thinking.
